# EP-1051

## Problem Statement
Is it true that if $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$ is a sequence of integers with\[\liminf a_n^{1/2^n}>1\]then\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_na_{n+1}}\]is irrational?

## Site Remarks
In \cite{Er88c} Erd\H{o}s notes this is true if $a_n\to \infty$ 'rapidly'. In \cite{ErGr80} they further ask 'what the strongest theorem of this type' would be.

This was solved in the affirmative by Aletheia \cite{Fe26}. This was extended by Barreto, Kang, Kim, Kova\v{c}, and Zhang \cite{BKKKZ26}, who essentially give a complete answer: if $\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ is the golden ratio and $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$ is a monotonically increasing sequence of integers such that\[\limsup a_n^{1/\phi^{n}}=\infty\]then\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_na_{n+1}}\]is irrational. Conversely, for any $1<C<\infty$ there exists a sequence of integers $1\leq a_1<\cdots$ such that\[\lim a_n^{1/\phi^{n}}=C\]where this infinite sum is a rational number. (Further, more general, results are available in \cite{BKKKZ26}.)

## Site References
- [BKKKZ26] K. Barreto, J. Kang, S.-H. Kim, V. Kova\v{c}, and S. Zhang, Irrationality of rapidly converging series: a problem of Erd\H{o}s and Graham. arXiv:2601.21442 (2026).
- [Er88c] Erd\H{o}s, P., On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results. New advances in transcendence theory (Durham, 1986) (1988), 102-109.

- [Fe26] T. Feng et al, Semi-Autonomous Mathematics Discovery with Gemini: A Case Study on the Erd\H{o}s Problems. arXiv:2601.22401 (2026).

- 16:35 on 30 Jan 2026 - TerenceTao (reply depth 1):
  A small heuristic as to the provenance of the golden ratio $\phi$: suppose that the $a_n$ exhibited double exponential growth $a_n \approx \exp(c^n)$ with some exponent $c>1$. Then any finite sum $\sum_{n=1}^N \frac{1}{a_n a_{n+1}}$ is a rational with denominator at most
  $$a_1 \dots a_{N+1} \approx \exp( c + c^2 + \dots + c^{N+1} ) \approx \exp( c^{N+1} / (1-1/c) )$$
  while the rapid decay of the summands means that the tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty \frac{1}{a_n a_{n+1}}$ has size about
  $$ \approx \frac{1}{a_{N+1}a_{N+2}} \approx \frac{1}{\exp( c^{N+1} + c^{N+2} )}.$$
  To make the finite sum converge to a rational, one therefore morally needs $c^{N+1} + c^{N+2} \leq c^{N+1} / (1-1/c)$ (ignoring some asymptotically negligible lower order terms) which after cancelling $c^{N+1}$ and performing some algebra becomes $c \leq \phi$. The arguments in the paper can be viewed as a rigorous version of the above heuristics (and their generalizations to other sums of this type).

## Local Computation
- finite proxy using model sequences of doubly-exponential scale
\[
a_n\approx c^{2^n},\quad c>1,
\]
and sums of reciprocal terms.
- For each model, computed high-precision numerical sums with tiny tail proxies and searched for close rationals by:
 - continued fractions (large denominator cap),
 - brute nearest-rational scan up to a large denominator threshold.

- Across tested growth bases, no small-denominator rational matched at the tail-resolved scale.
- This supports the irrationality heuristic but does not prove the theorem-level statement.

## Local Proof Attempts
Target:
Prove irrationality under the weaker growth hypothesis
\[
\liminf a_n^{1/2^n}>1.
\]
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Show a quantitative rational-approximation barrier: under the liminf condition, truncation tails satisfy
\[
\left|x-\frac{p}{q}\right|>\frac{1}{q^{2+\eta}}
\]
for all large \(q\) and some \(\eta>0\), excluding eventual periodic/too-good rational approximants.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (tail control from growth):
If \(a_n\ge (1+\delta)^{2^n}\) eventually, then reciprocal tails decay doubly exponentially.
Proof.
\(1/a_n\le (1+\delta)^{-2^n}\); geometric summation of doubly exponential terms gives tiny tails. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (continued-fraction obstruction):
If a real number is rational, continued fraction expansion terminates, so approximation error by convergents drops to \(0\) exactly at finite stage.
Proof.
Standard continued fraction characterization of rationals. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies irrationality):
If A forbids all sufficiently strong rational approximants compatible with eventual termination, then \(x\) cannot be rational.
Proof.
Rationality would produce exact finite termination and hence perfect approximation beyond some stage, contradicting A. \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is upgrading tail smallness from liminf growth into a uniform Diophantine-approximation exclusion theorem strong enough to force irrationality in full generality.
